title: 1st Abyss 1st Matter In Universal Questions Denial Is Worthless Against Proof

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the passage?
questions.answer: It warns about two major causes of doubt in faith in this age and explains how to be protected from them.

questions.question: How is the discussion organized at the beginning of the passage?
questions.answer: It is presented through four questions, but this section gives two key matters connected to the first danger.

questions.question: What is the first danger described in the passage?
questions.answer: It is a kind of doubt that weakens firm faith and makes people hesitate.

questions.question: In the first matter, how is proof compared with denial in general issues?
questions.answer: Proof is strong and meaningful, while denial is weak and carries little value against clear evidence.

questions.question: What example is used to show the strength of proof over denial?
questions.answer: The passage uses the example of seeing the new moon at the start of Ramadan.

questions.question: Why do two people who confirm something strengthen each other?
questions.answer: Because they point to the same real thing and their testimonies come together in support of one truth.

questions.question: Why do many people who deny something not necessarily strengthen one another?
questions.answer: Because each denial comes from that person’s own limited view, so their statements remain separate.

questions.question: According to the passage, what is difficult about proving that something does not exist anywhere?
questions.answer: It would require searching everywhere and across all times, which is far harder than showing that something exists.

questions.question: What mistake do deniers make when they judge only by themselves?
questions.answer: They confuse their own lack of seeing with the claim that the thing is not real at all.

questions.question: Why is a sweeping denial in matters of belief described as extremely serious?
questions.answer: Because belief-related matters concern the whole universe, so denying them completely is a huge and false claim.

questions.question: What short conclusion is given after the first matter?
questions.answer: Statements that affirm truth unite around one result, but denials split into many separate claims.

questions.question: Why should the large number of unbelievers not shake a believer’s confidence, according to the passage?
questions.answer: Because quantity does not make denial stronger when those denials cannot truly support each other.

questions.question: What two major faith-related problems does this passage begin to address?
questions.answer: It begins to address two deep sources of doubt that disturb certainty in belief.

questions.question: Why does the passage not fully re-explain the truth mentioned at the start?
questions.answer: Because it says that truth has already been firmly demonstrated elsewhere, so only the main dangers are summarized here.

questions.question: What is the first protective lesson given against doubt?
questions.answer: It teaches that denial is weak when it stands against genuine proof.

questions.question: How does the Ramadan moon example help explain this lesson?
questions.answer: It shows that a small number of witnesses who truly saw something can outweigh many who only say they did not see it.

questions.question: In that example, why does not seeing the moon fail to cancel the testimony of those who saw it?
questions.answer: Because failing to see something is not the same as proving it was not there.

questions.question: When people affirm a fact, what happens to their testimonies?
questions.answer: Their testimonies come together and support one another.

questions.question: When people deny a fact, why do their statements remain weak?
questions.answer: Each one speaks only from personal limits, so their claims do not merge into one strong proof.

questions.question: What does the passage say would be required to prove that something never existed?
questions.answer: A person would need complete knowledge of every place and every period of time.

questions.question: What is wrong with saying, “I do not see it, so it is not really there”?
questions.answer: That turns a personal limitation into a claim about reality, which is not justified.

questions.question: Why is total denial in matters of faith described as especially false?
questions.answer: Because these matters are vast and connected to all existence, so a complete denial goes far beyond what a person can know.

questions.question: What contrast is made between affirmation and negation in the short summary after the first matter?
questions.answer: Affirmation leads to one shared result, while negation breaks apart into many separate results.

questions.question: What comfort does the passage offer believers when they see many deniers?
questions.answer: It reminds them that large numbers do not make unsupported denial true or strong.

questions.question: What overall issue is the passage concerned with?
questions.answer: It is concerned with protecting certainty of faith from doubts and denials.

questions.question: How many major helps for escaping the first abyss are explained in this passage?
questions.answer: Two major helps are explained.

questions.question: What is the key claim of the first matter?
questions.answer: In broad issues, denial has little force when it is faced with actual evidence.

questions.question: What religious example is used to make that claim easier to understand?
questions.answer: The example of confirming the new moon for the beginning of Ramadan is used.

questions.question: In that example, whose statement carries stronger weight and why?
questions.answer: The statement of those who saw the moon carries stronger weight because it rests on direct witness.

questions.question: Why does simple non-observation not amount to proof of absence?
questions.answer: Because not seeing something may come from one’s own limitation rather than the thing’s nonexistence.

questions.question: How does the passage explain the strength of those who affirm?
questions.answer: It says they are joined by one objective reality, so they reinforce each other.

questions.question: How does the passage explain the weakness of those who deny?
questions.answer: It says they remain divided because each denial comes from a separate personal viewpoint.

questions.question: What would someone have to do to truly prove absolute nonexistence?
questions.answer: That person would have to investigate all places and all times completely.

questions.question: What does the passage imply about human ability to make such an absolute denial?
questions.answer: It implies that human beings are not able to make that kind of complete judgement honestly.

questions.question: Why is denial in matters of belief more dangerous than in small everyday issues?
questions.answer: Because belief concerns realities as wide as the whole universe, so false denial there has massive consequences.

questions.question: What does the passage say about the apparent majority of deniers?
questions.answer: Their greater number does not give real weight to their position.

questions.question: What does the passage say has already happened elsewhere regarding the truth under discussion?
questions.answer: It says the truth has already been established with strong evidence in another work.

questions.question: Why does the passage still continue the discussion if that proof already exists elsewhere?
questions.answer: Because it wants to highlight two major sources of hesitation that disturb faith in the present age.

questions.question: What first idea is taught for rescue from the first source of hesitation?
questions.answer: It teaches that denial is weak and cannot stand against real proof.

questions.question: How does the example of the Ramadan crescent support that idea?
questions.answer: It shows that direct witness from even a small number can be stronger than many people merely reporting no sighting.

questions.question: What does the passage suggest about the difference between witnessing and failing to witness?
questions.answer: Witnessing gives positive evidence, while failing to witness does not settle the issue.

questions.question: Why do affirming statements naturally gather strength?
questions.answer: Because they point to one shared reality and so support each other.

questions.question: Why do denying statements fail to gather the same strength?
questions.answer: Because each one is tied to the denier’s own limits and does not become a united proof.

questions.question: What would be necessary to justify a claim that something is nowhere to be found and never existed?
questions.answer: A complete search of the whole world and all past times would be necessary.

questions.question: What personal phrase does the passage connect with weak denial?
questions.answer: It connects weak denial with statements based only on one’s own opinion or belief.

questions.question: Why can such personal denial not become a final judgement about reality?
questions.answer: Because private perception cannot cover all that is real.

questions.question: What does the short summary after the first matter say about the result of affirmation?
questions.answer: It says affirmation has one unified outcome.

questions.question: What does it say about the result of negation?
questions.answer: It says negation has many scattered outcomes.

questions.question: What age-related problem is the passage trying to respond to?
questions.answer: It is responding to modern doubts that shake certainty in faith.

questions.question: How much of the larger subject does this passage say it will cover?
questions.answer: It says it will mention only part of the issue, focusing on two deep causes of hesitation.

questions.question: What is the first matter mainly arguing?
questions.answer: It argues that proof has real force, while denial in general matters is weak.

questions.question: Which example from Islamic life is used to explain this argument?
questions.answer: The example used is the sighting of the Ramadan crescent.

questions.question: In that example, why does the report of a few witnesses matter more than many denials?
questions.answer: Because the witnesses give positive evidence of what they actually observed.

questions.question: What happens when one person who affirms is joined by another who points to the same truth?
questions.answer: Their statements become mutually supporting and stronger.

questions.question: Why does denial remain isolated even when many people repeat it?
questions.answer: Because each person is only expressing a separate lack of perception.

questions.question: What kind of effort would be needed to establish that something does not exist at all?
questions.answer: A total investigation of all places and all historical periods would be needed.

questions.question: What important distinction does the passage make between “I do not see” and “it does not exist”?
questions.answer: The first is about personal experience, while the second is a universal claim that goes far beyond that experience.

questions.question: Why is making a universal denial in belief matters especially reckless?
questions.answer: Because those matters include the whole cosmos and cannot be measured by one person’s limited view.

questions.question: What is the basic takeaway of the first short summary?
questions.answer: Positive testimony gathers into one strong line, but denials split into separate lines that do not unite.

questions.question: How should a believer view the apparent numerical strength of deniers?
questions.answer: A believer should not treat it as meaningful proof against faith.

questions.question: What is being threatened in this passage by the “abysses” of the age?
questions.answer: Firm certainty in faith is being threatened.

questions.question: What method does the passage use to discuss this issue briefly?
questions.answer: It treats the issue through a structured set of questions and answers, then focuses here on two matters.

questions.question: What lesson stands at the center of the first matter?
questions.answer: The central lesson is that denial is weak when clear proof is present.

questions.question: Why is the moon-sighting example a strong fit for this lesson?
questions.answer: Because it clearly separates direct evidence from mere absence of observation.

questions.question: What does the passage show about the relation between those who confirm a truth?
questions.answer: They share one reality, so each one adds strength to the others.

questions.question: What does it show about the relation between those who deny a truth?
questions.answer: They do not unite in the same way because each one is limited by a different barrier or blind spot.

questions.question: How does the passage explain the heavy burden on someone trying to prove nonexistence?
questions.answer: It says such a person would need total knowledge covering the whole world and all ages.

questions.question: What kind of statement is acceptable for a limited denier to make about personal experience?
questions.answer: The denier may honestly say that he himself does not see the thing.

questions.question: What kind of statement does the passage reject as false in major belief matters?
questions.answer: It rejects the claim that something is not real in itself simply because one person does not perceive it.

questions.question: Why are these false denials described as enormous?
questions.answer: Because they make claims as wide as the world without having the knowledge required for them.

questions.question: What contrast between affirmation and negation is emphasized in the first summary?
questions.answer: Affirmation gathers into one shared conclusion, while negation breaks into many private conclusions.

questions.question: How does this contrast answer the pressure created by large numbers of deniers?
questions.answer: It shows that their number is misleading because their denials do not combine into a single solid proof.
